title: Tables, rows and keys
summary: Why Notely outgrows one big file, and how a database keeps notes in tables, gives every row a key, and links rows together.
youWillLearn: Why an app outgrows "one big file", and what a database does instead
How tables, rows and columns map to the things in your app
What a primary key is, and why it should never mean anything
How a foreign key links a note to its owner, and guards that link

glossary.app server: A computer, somewhere else, that runs the app's own code. Notely's runs on Vercel.
glossary.database: A program built to store data safely and find it again fast.
glossary.relational database: A database that keeps data in tables and links rows across tables by their keys. Postgres is one.
glossary.Postgres: PostgreSQL, a free and very widely used relational database. Supabase runs one for Notely.
glossary.table: A named collection of rows that all describe the same kind of thing, like users or notes.
glossary.row: One entry in a table: one user, one note.
glossary.column: One named, typed fact that every row in a table has, like title or created_at.
glossary.primary key: The column whose value is different for every row and never changes, so the row can always be found again.
glossary.foreign key: A column that stores the primary key of a row in another table, and that the database checks really exists.
glossary.constraint: A rule on a column, like not null or unique, that the database checks on every save.

steps.title: Notely keeps every note in one file
body: Notely is the notes app we build in this course. Today it has one user, Maya, with three notes.
When Maya saves a note, the app server (the computer running Notely's code) writes it into one file: a single list of every note. To show her a note, it reads the list until it finds it.

callout.text: New to Notely? The 4-minute Meet Notely lesson at the start of this module shows the whole app, part by part.

scene.caption: Maya's notes go through the app server into one file.

steps.title: Ten thousand users, one fragile file
body: Notely grows to 10,000 users and two million notes. To show Maya one note, the server now reads through every note anyone ever wrote.
Worse, when two people save at the same moment, both rewrite the file, and the second write wipes out the first. Saves quietly disappear.

callout.text: A shoebox of receipts. Fine for ten. With two million, finding one means tipping the whole box onto the floor.

scene.caption: Every request reads the whole file, and saves collide.

steps.title: A database instead of a file
body: The fix is a database: a program built to store data safely and find it fast. Notely uses Postgres, run for us by Supabase.
Postgres lets thousands of people save at the same moment without losing anything. It is a relational database: it keeps data in tables, one per kind of thing.
changes: + Database: Postgres, run for us by Supabase

scene.caption: The file is gone. The app server talks to a database.

steps.title: Rows are things, columns are facts
body: Let's look inside the database. A table is like a spreadsheet with strict rules. Each row is one thing: one note. Each column is one fact about it: its title, its owner, when it was made.
Every column has a fixed type. A created_at column only takes dates, so "next week-ish" cannot sneak in.
changes: − 10,000 users, App Server and Database: we zoom inside
+ notes table with three rows: Groceries, Book ideas, Trip plan

scene.caption: The notes table: one row per note.

steps.title: Every row needs a name tag
body: Two notes can share a title, so a title cannot tell rows apart. Each table gets a primary key: one column, usually id, whose value is different for every row and never changes.
Postgres keeps the keys sorted, like the index of a book. Finding note 102 means checking one row, not two million.
changes: ~ Trip plan renamed Groceries: same title, different id

scene.caption: Two notes called Groceries, told apart by their ids.

steps.title: Keys that point at other tables
body: Users get a table too: Maya's row has id 7, Leo's has id 8. Each note stores its owner's id in a column called user_id. A column that holds another table's primary key is a foreign key.
Postgres guards the link: it refuses a note for user 99 when user 99 does not exist.
changes: + users table with two rows: Maya and Leo
+ Arrows: each note's user_id points at its owner

scene.caption: Each note points at exactly one user.

steps.title: Notely's first two tables, in SQL
body: Here is the same picture as real code. Pasted into the Supabase SQL editor, it creates both tables, both primary keys and the link between them.
Read each line like a form field: a name, a type, then rules like not null (must be filled). Rules like these are called constraints.

code.caption: references users (id) is the foreign key. Real Supabase apps get users from Supabase Auth, with uuid ids; lesson 6 shows how.

changes: ~ Same two tables, now written as SQL on the right

scene.caption: Two create table statements: two tables, two keys, one link.

steps.title: Do not use a fact as the key
body: Tempting: make Maya's email the primary key of users. It is unique, after all.

Then Maya changes her email. Every note that stored the old address must change too, or Postgres refuses the update. Keys should be boring numbers that never need to change. Keep the email as a normal column with a unique rule.

callout.text: When Claude Code creates tables, check: does every table have a primary key? Is each link a real references, not a plain number column? Ask it to show the final create table SQL.

changes: ~ Her notes' links break when the email changes

scene.caption: With the email as the key, changing it breaks every link to Maya.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: A relational database is a set of tables. Rows are things, columns are typed facts. A primary key names each row for good. A foreign key stores another row's key, and Postgres keeps those links honest.
The rest of this module, from joins to migrations, builds on these four ideas.

scene.caption: Tables, rows, a key on every row, and checked links between them.

quiz.question: Notely's notes table has the columns id, user_id and title. Which one is the foreign key?

options.why: That is the primary key: it names this note. It does not point anywhere else.
It stores the primary key of a row in another table, users. That is exactly what a foreign key is.
The title is an ordinary fact about the note. Two notes can even share one.

quiz.question: Claude Code proposes a users table whose primary key is the email column. What do you ask for?

options.text: Keep it. Emails are unique, so they make a fine key.
options.why: Unique is not enough. A key must also never change, and people change their email.

options.text: Drop the unique rule on email, so changing it is easier.
options.why: That would allow two accounts with the same email. The fix is a different key, not a weaker rule.

options.text: A generated id as the primary key, and email as a unique column.
options.why: The id has no meaning, so it never needs to change. Email stays unique, and can change without breaking any links.

quiz.question: A bug in Notely tries to save a note with user_id = 99, but there is no user 99. The foreign key is declared. What happens?

options.text: Postgres rejects the save with an error.
options.why: A foreign key means the row it points at must exist. The bad write never lands, so the bug shows up instead of hiding.

options.text: The note is saved and never shows up for anyone.
options.why: That is what happens without a foreign key: orphan rows that quietly pile up.

options.text: Postgres creates an empty user 99 to keep things consistent.
options.why: Databases never invent rows for you. A rule can only accept or refuse a write.

takeaways: A relational database is a set of tables: one per kind of thing, one row per thing, one typed column per fact.
Every table needs a primary key: unique, never changing, with no meaning of its own.
A foreign key (references) links rows across tables, and Postgres refuses links to rows that do not exist.
Put rules like not null and unique in the database, not only in app code.
